content: Sick newborns and preterm infants often cannot be fed through the gastrointestinal tract and require parenteral nutrition. While higher parenteral amino acid (AA) intake may improve nitrogen balance, growth, and overall health, there are concerns about whether newborns can effectively metabolize high levels of amino acids, particularly in the early days after birth. The primary goal of this study was to evaluate whether a higher intake of parenteral amino acids, compared to a lower intake, improves growth and survival without disability in newborns receiving parenteral nutrition. Secondary objectives included assessing whether higher amino acid intake at the start or at its maximum level improves growth and survival without adverse effects. Additionally, the study examined whether increased amino acid intake should replace, supplement, or be provided alongside non-protein energy sources like glucose and lipids. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore differences in outcomes based on gestational age, birth weight, timing of amino acid initiation, infant condition, and fluid intake. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, up to June 2017. They also reviewed clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and article citations. Only randomized controlled trials comparing higher versus lower amino acid intake in parenteral nutrition for newborns were included. Comparisons were made for higher intake at the start, at maximum levels, and at both stages. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Fixed-effect analyses were performed, and treatment effects were expressed as mean differences (MD), risk ratios (RR), and risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 32 studies met the inclusion criteria. Of these, six were short-term studies on biochemical tolerance, one involved infants born after 35 weeks of gestation, one focused on term surgical newborns, and three provided no usable data. The remaining 21 studies reported clinical outcomes in very preterm or low birth weight infants and were included in the meta-analysis. Higher amino acid intake did not significantly affect mortality before hospital discharge (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.17; 1407 participants; 14 studies; low-quality evidence). There was insufficient evidence to demonstrate an effect on neurodevelopment, with no reported benefits (very low-quality evidence). However, higher amino acid intake was associated with a reduction in postnatal growth failure (defined as growth below the 10th percentile) at discharge (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.97; 203 participants; 3 studies; very low-quality evidence). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of postnatal growth failure was 7 (95% CI 4 to 50). Subgroup analyses suggested that reduced growth failure was observed in infants who started on higher amino acid intake (2 to 3 g/kg/day), received increased amino acid and non-protein caloric intake, began intake within 24 hours of birth, or received early lipid infusion. Higher amino acid intake was associated with a shorter time to regain birth weight (MD -1.14 days, 95% CI -1.73 to -0.56; 950 participants; 13 studies). However, the effects on other growth parameters were inconsistent, with no clear impact on anthropometric z-scores at any time point. There was an increase in head circumference growth at discharge (MD 0.09 cm/week, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.13; 315 participants; 4 studies; very low-quality evidence). Higher amino acid intake did not affect the time to achieve full enteral feeding, the incidence of late-onset sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, chronic lung disease, intraventricular hemorrhage (any or severe), or periventricular leukomalacia. However, it was associated with a reduction in retinopathy of prematurity (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.93; 269 participants; 4 studies; very low-quality evidence), though there was no difference in the incidence of severe retinopathy of prematurity. Biochemically, higher amino acid intake was linked to an increase in positive protein and nitrogen balance. However, it also raised the risk of biochemical intolerance, such as elevated blood urea nitrogen levels (RR 2.77, 95% CI 2.13 to 3.61; 688 participants; 7 studies; high-quality evidence). The number needed to harm (NNH) for this outcome was 4 (95% CI 3 to 5). Higher amino acid intake was associated with a reduction in hyperglycemia (blood glucose > 8.3 mmol/L) (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.96; 505 participants; 5 studies), although there was no difference in the incidence of hyperglycemia requiring insulin treatment. In conclusion, low-quality evidence suggests that higher amino acid intake in parenteral nutrition does not affect mortality. Very low-quality evidence indicates that it may reduce postnatal growth failure and retinopathy of prematurity, though not severe retinopathy. There was insufficient evidence to demonstrate an effect on neurodevelopment. Higher amino acid intake was associated with potential adverse biochemical effects, such as azotemia, due to excessive amino acid load. Further well-powered trials in very preterm infants are needed to determine the optimal amino acid intake and the effects of caloric balance in parenteral nutrition on brain development and neurodevelopmental outcomes.
